storm.summary_layperson: Bands of heavy rain and gusty east winds are moving over the cove right now, with a stronger cell about 5 miles west due in around 4:10 PM; thunder is unlikely, and the Sound offers no extra protection tonight, so the cove gets the same soaking as the surrounding towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer tonight: the Sound (58°F) is already about 10°F warmer than the air, and the gap only widens to ~11°F by 6 PM as the air cools.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: a coastal low is passing south of Long Island Sound, spreading widespread rain over the area with a strong east wind. KOKX radar shows many rain cores within 10 miles of the cove; the strongest nearby is a 46 dBZ cell about 5 miles west, moving east-northeast at about 17 kt and due over the cove around 4:10 PM. Weaker cells (36–38 dBZ) are already overhead or just southwest, and RYC is recording rain now. No NWS watches or warnings are in effect.

Why the risk is high but the hazard is rain and wind, not thunder: heavy cells this close count as high risk on this page whatever their type. But instability is essentially zero (CAPE 0–10 J/kg), so these are heavy rain showers rather than thunderstorms; lightning is unlikely. Wind shear is strong (about 53 kt), which helps stronger cores bring gusts down. The Western Sound buoy has gusted to 36 kt out of the east, and gusts of 18–21 kt are reaching the Old Greenwich shore. Earlier this afternoon a round of storms over NYC briefly turned severe, but the NWS says that round has weakened.

Local modifier — none tonight: the Sound usually blunts storms when its water is much colder than the air, because cool water keeps a stable layer of air near the surface. Tonight it is the other way round: the water is 58°F and the air is 48–50°F, so the water is about 10°F warmer. There is no stable layer, and the air keeps cooling (gap about −11°F by 6 PM), so none will form during the window. With the sun down at 4:38 PM and no sea breeze, nothing local slows or weakens the rain bands. Expect the cove to get the same weather as Stamford, Rye and Port Chester.

Most likely outcome: steady to heavy rain showers through the evening, with the NWS putting rain chances at about 90% until 10 PM and adding a quarter to half an inch. The east wind stays strong and gusty, with its strongest gusts inside the heavier cells. The nearest cell's predicted arrival time has already passed, so check live radar for what is overhead right now rather than relying on a timed ETA.

What would change the call: a severe thunderstorm warning, or any lightning, would mean the earlier NYC-style storms were redeveloping. Downgrade once the rain shield moves northeast of Stamford and the heavy cores (45+ dBZ) are gone from the western Sound.

wind.regime_label: Moderate gradient wind from a passing coastal low — no sea breeze
wind.tactics_blurb: A strong, rainy east-northeast breeze that slowly turns to the left (counterclockwise) through the evening; the eastern half of the course near Tod's Point sits in its wind shadow. Favor the left (northern, upper-cove) side and expect the persistent left shift to keep paying.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Wind type: moderate gradient wind — no sea breeze in play. A coastal low passing south of the Sound is driving the wind. The sun sets at 4:38 PM, before the window opens, and the Sound (58°F) is about 10°F warmer than the air, so there is no sea breeze at all. The sea-breeze direction correction does not apply.

Direction — the model and the shore disagree: the HRRR model has the cove at NE (45–48°), while the NWS hourly forecast says E. Observations sit between them: RYC reads ENE 66°, the Western Sound stations average about ENE 75°, and Old Greenwich is ENE 63°. Station agreement is only moderate (0.68). The forecast uses the observed ENE (~65°) as its baseline, then turns it slowly left toward NE after 8 PM as the low pulls away northeast. The NWS has NE by midnight. Read this as a persistent left shift, not oscillation.

Where the pressure is: an east-northeast wind is part-sheltered by the Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) peninsula on the east side of the cove mouth. The open Sound is far windier than the cove: the buoy reads 26 kt gusting 36, while the RYC 10-minute average is 8.6 kt with gusts to 18. Pressure is lighter and patchier on the east shore near Tod's Point, and fuller up the cove and to the left. As the wind backs toward NE, flow through the cove gets cleaner and more even.

Tactics: start toward the left end and work the left (northern) side on the first beat. You get the persistent backing shift and stay out of the Tod's Point shadow. Expect sudden gusts and brief direction jumps of 10–20° as each rain cell passes; tack on the big headers, but don't give up the left side for a puff-induced lift on the right.

What the fleet will feel: a sustained 12–15 kt with gusts of 18–24 kt from 6 to 8 PM, in steady to heavy rain after dark with air around 50°F. That's a full-hiking, reefed or depowered breeze for small boats, and cold and wet for everyone. Speeds after 6 PM come from the NWS hourly forecast because the model data stops there, so the details for 7–10 PM are less certain.

Marine-layer trend only covers through 6 PM for the same reason; it shows no buffer at any hour, so the gap doesn't matter tonight
